title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Dust and the Light

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a deep dive into one of the greatest, and perhaps most underrated, novels in the English language.

Our Mutual Friend was Charles Dickens's last completed novel, published in 1865, and it is an astonishing thing — sprawling, dark, wildly funny, and shot through with a moral urgency that feels entirely modern.
Over this series, we'll be unpacking its great themes — money, identity, reinvention, the river that runs beneath everything — passage by passage, chapter by chapter.
Today we begin at the beginning: the dust and the light — the novel's peculiar atmosphere, and the extraordinary mystery at its heart.
I'm joined by three remarkable readers, each of whom brings a different set of obsessions to the text.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing professor who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a movement — she sees every gear and spring, and she finds the architecture thrilling.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes the novel's genius is moral before it is social — he reads character with forensic patience and quotes Dr Johnson with alarming frequency.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite recovered — she comes to the text with both a scholar's care and a reader's unguarded love.
Welcome, all three of you.
Let's start with the novel's central puzzle: John Harmon.

A young man who inherits a fortune, arrives in England, fakes his own death, and then moves invisibly through the story under a false name, watching — watching Bella Wilfer, watching the Boffins, watching himself.
Eleanor, you've been thinking about how Dickens constructs John Harmon's interiority — his self-examination — in the great soliloquy of chapter thirty.
What does it feel like, as a piece of writing?
It feels like nothing else in Victorian fiction — and I mean that precisely.
Dickens gives us John Harmon working through his own past in real time, almost interrogating himself, as though he doesn't quite trust his own memory.
There's a structural tic Dickens deploys here that I find quite brilliant: the self-correction.
Harmon asks himself, 'Is that so?' and then immediately answers, 'That is exactly so.'
It's a mind verifying its own testimony — like a witness in a courtroom who also happens to be the judge.
And then there's the extraordinary accumulation of that central sentence — listen to how it builds.
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
That repeated 'shrinking' — it's not decoration, it's a physical sensation.
The word enacts what it describes — a man recoiling from his own inheritance, from his own name.
I think Eleanor is right to fix on the moral weight of that sentence, though I'd frame it slightly differently.
What strikes me is not the technique, but the character it reveals.
Harmon is a young man who has been left a great fortune and finds it, quite genuinely, a burden rather than a blessing.
That is not a sociological observation about the corrupting nature of wealth — it is a portrait of a conscience.
He fears, quite specifically, that money is already making him avaricious — that the disease has begun before he even knows it.
Dickens calls it 'mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious' — that adverb 'already' is the knife in the sentence.
It suggests the corruption is not hypothetical but present — quietly underway, like rot in timber.
What moves me about this passage — and I come back to it every time I re-read the novel — is the tenderness at its edges.
Harmon speaks of 'the two dear noble honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life.'
Those Boffins — those warm, unglamorous, utterly good people — are named here only as sunlight.
There's no irony in it, no qualification — and in a novel as ironically dense as this one, that simplicity is almost startling.
And then Dickens mentions 'my heartbroken sister' — one phrase, no more.
This sister barely appears in the novel, and yet the weight of her grief is carried in those two words.
That connects beautifully to the second passage — because Dickens immediately moves from this raw self-examination to something altogether more plotted and practical.
Harmon explains how he and this stranger, Radfoot, hatched their scheme — to disguise themselves as sailors and observe Bella Wilfer from close quarters.
The plan, as Dickens renders it, sounds almost boyish — impulsive, makeshift.
Dickens writes it with that characteristic lightness — let me find the line.
'The plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'
'Throwing ourselves' — it's such an ungainly, almost comic phrase for something so consequential.
The whole architecture of the novel — the disguise, the identity, the inheritance — rests on a plan two men cooked up in a deck cabin because they happened to have attended school in Brussels.
I confess the contrivance of that plot has always tested my patience slightly — though Dickens earns it, eventually.
What interests me more is what the scheme reveals about Harmon's state of mind.
He wants to know whether Bella Wilfer is mercenary before he presents himself — he wants to test her character anonymously, from a safe remove.
There is something both admirable and slightly cowardly in that impulse — and Dickens, I think, sees both things clearly.
Note that Harmon says, 'God only knows how much of it true, and how much of it false' — about Radfoot's personal history.
That parenthesis is a warning sign the reader is invited to notice and Harmon, at the time, did not.
Edmund's right, and it makes the whole scheme feel poignant rather than merely clever.
Harmon is trying to find solid ground — to know one true thing about his future before he steps into it.
And the irony is that he places his trust in a man who is himself a fabrication, a mirror of false histories.
The whole novel is threaded with that — people performing selves they have invented, or selves that have been thrust upon them.
Which brings us, rather naturally, to Charley Hexam — who performs a self he has constructed with enormous effort, only to find it cracking under him.
The passage from chapter fifty-seven — Charley confronting Bradley Headstone — is one of the coldest, most uncomfortable scenes in the novel.
Charley has clawed his way out of his origins — he is educated, ambitious, respectable — and now he sees all of that threatened by Bradley's violence.
And his complaint is not moral outrage — it is something far more self-interested and therefore more honest.
He says to Bradley — and this is extraordinary — 'how do you know that, pursuing the ends of your own violent temper, you have not laid me open to suspicion?'
His entire grievance is reputational — not that a man has been nearly murdered, but that Charley's good name might be smirched by association.
Dickens gives him no redemptive irony — Charley means every word, and that is damning.
Charley Hexam is one of Dickens's most uncomfortable portraits, I agree — because he is neither villain nor victim.
He is a morally mediocre man in circumstances that demand moral greatness.

The detail that stings is this — he says to Headstone: 'You know that I took you with me to his chambers in the Temple when I told him my opinion of you, and made myself responsible for my opinion of you.'
He vouched for Bradley.
He put his own credibility behind a man he should have seen more clearly.
That is not merely unfortunate — it is a failure of judgment, and Dickens treats it as such.
What I find so uncomfortable — and I mean that as the highest compliment — is the syntax of Charley's accusation.
Dickens builds it with those careful qualifications — 'if you had any part, I don't say what' — 'if you know anything about it, I don't say how much.'
Charley is not accusing Bradley outright — he is circling, insinuating, protecting himself even in the act of confrontation.
And then he closes with that almost breathtaking question: 'Is that your gratitude to me, Mr Headstone?'
The moral universe has been entirely reduced to the question of what Charley Hexam is owed.
And there, I think, we find one of the novel's great recurring notes — the question of what we are owed, and what we owe, and how those two calculations can corrupt a person entirely.
We'll be returning to Charley, and to Bradley, and to Lizzie — who is caught between them both — throughout this series.
But coming up next: the river itself — that great, dark, indifferent Thames that opens the novel and never quite leaves it.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Bella's Ascent: From Mercenary to Human

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We're deep in the novel's moral architecture today, following the characters who are tested, transformed, or destroyed by their circumstances.
Our subject is Bella's ascent — and the constellation of characters whose redemptions, sacrifices, and deceptions orbit around her.
With me today: Dr. Eleanor Hartley, who reads Dickens as a master architect of prose and plot.
Sir Edmund Leigh, who insists — rightly, I think — that this novel is finally about moral character, not social conditions.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt, who has lived with this novel since girlhood and never quite stopped rereading it.
Let's begin with John Harmon's extraordinary act of self-erasure — the decision to remain dead in order to prove Bella.
What strikes me first about Harmon's decision is how Dickens frames it — not as heroic resolution, but as something that crept up on him.
There's a passage in the later chapter that captures this with devastating precision.
'He had lapsed into the condition in which he found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances.'
That phrase — 'accumulative power of its separate circumstances' — is doing extraordinary moral work.
Dickens is saying: human entrapment rarely arrives as a sudden catastrophe.
It accretes, the way silt accretes on a riverbed — which is perfectly apt for this novel, of all novels.
Eleanor puts that well, and I'd only add that Dickens is equally precise about the origin of the distrust.
This is not a man who distrusts Bella out of cynicism or calculation.
The text is quite specific about where the wound comes from.
'The distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence.'
That parenthetical — 'never yet for good within his knowledge then' — is the key to Harmon's entire story.
The word 'then' quietly promises that the knowledge will come — that goodness will eventually be witnessed.
And it does, in the form of the Boffins.
What moves me in that same passage is the impossible bind Dickens places Harmon in.
He cannot come to life without either buying Bella or punishing her.
There's no moral exit — except through her transformation.
And what I find tender in the earlier passage — his night in the public-house — is that the plan to prove Bella is born from love, not suspicion.
He's trying to spare her from the fate that 'should lead to nothing but evil' — his father's money, the perpetuating curse.
'The dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches — the fate that they should lead to nothing but evil.'
He is trying, in his painfully indirect way, to act well.
That's exactly right, and it illuminates how Dickens structures the whole arc — the deception that begins well and then spirals beyond intention.
There's also a wonderful structural rhyme with Lizzie Hexam, who is doing something parallel — sacrificing herself in the hope of transforming the man she loves.
The passage where she speaks — as though through the voice of another — about Eugene is almost unbearably generous.
'Only put me in that empty place, only try how little I mind myself, only prove what a world of things I will do and bear for you.'
That triple 'only' — it's a rhetorical plea, yes, but it's also structurally mimetic.
Each 'only' reduces her further — she is asking to be diminished so he might grow larger.
I'd gently resist the word 'sacrifice' as though Lizzie were merely an instrument of Eugene's redemption.
Dickens is drawing something finer than that.
Lizzie says, with perfect clarity, that Eugene has failings — but that those failings grew from want of something to trust in.
This is the moral insight that Dr. Johnson calls charity in its deepest sense — seeing the cause of vice before condemning the vice itself.
And the hope she expresses — 'that you might even come to be much better than you are, through me who am so much worse' — that is not self-abasement.
'I hope that you might even come to be much better than you are, through me who am so much worse, and hardly worth the thinking of beside you.'
It is self-knowledge — and it is, in its own way, a form of moral courage.
Edmund, you make me hear that passage differently — and I'm grateful for it.
But I want to bring in Jenny Wren here, because she is the spiritual counter-weight to all this moral calculation.
Where Harmon and Lizzie struggle toward goodness through acts of will, Jenny simply has it — and she is also the one who suffers most purely.
Her vision of the celestial children — the 'long bright slanting rows' — is one of the most beautiful passages Dickens ever wrote.
'Who is this in pain! Who is this in pain!' When I told them who it was, they answered, 'Come and play with us!'
That repetition — the question asked twice — it doesn't feel like rhetoric.
It feels like a voice genuinely searching for her.
Caroline, you've touched on something I find essential about this novel's moral imagination.
Jenny Wren is not redeemed through the plot — she redeems others.
Her suffering is not explained or resolved — it is simply witnessed, and her vision is the reward for enduring it.
Dickens gives her the most extraordinary image for the experience of grace — not a theological argument, but a sensory memory.
'They swept about me and took me up, and made me light.'
Three verbs — swept, took, made — and a whole theology of deliverance in four words: 'made me light.'
Dickens knew that the most spiritually powerful moments in fiction resist explanation.
Edmund, that reading makes me want to put it alongside the Bradley Headstone passage — because the contrast is almost brutal.
Jenny is made light — Bradley is made old, is made ash.
The passage describing him through that terrible night is the dark photographic negative of Jenny's vision.
'Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face.'
Jenny's celestial children come down in 'long bright slanting rows' — Bradley sits before a fire that devours him.
Both passages are about light — but one is transcendence, the other is immolation.
That parallel is devastating when you see it.
And there's a detail in the Bradley passage I can't get out of my head — 'the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating.'
'Its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating.'
The body is becoming what he has done — the ash of destroyed lives.
It's almost Dorian Gray — except the portrait and the man are the same thing here.
Which brings us, I think, to the novel's resolution of the good souls — Harmon's tribute to the Boffins.
In the scene where Harmon confronts Wegg, he says something that strikes me as the moral thesis of the entire novel.
'I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness — there are no words to satisfy me — of Mr and Mrs Boffin.'
'There are no words to satisfy me' — that is Dickens testing language at its limit and admitting the test fails.
The novelist who found a word for everything concedes that genuine goodness exceeds vocabulary.
And that, I would argue, is not a failure of craft — it is its highest expression.
What a place to pause on — language failing at the threshold of goodness.
We've moved today from Harmon's night in a public-house to Jenny Wren's visionary children, from Lizzie's extraordinary act of faith to Bradley's disintegration by firelight.
What binds them, perhaps, is Dickens's conviction that character is always in motion — ascending or degenerating, but never fixed.
My thanks to Eleanor, Edmund, and Caroline — and we'll be back shortly with more from Our Mutual Friend.

segments.title: The Comedy of Dust: Greed and Transformation

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart — sentence by sentence, image by image — to see how it works and why it endures.
I'm joined today by three brilliant readers of this extraordinary book.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — with intense delight in the engineering.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes the novel's greatness lives in moral imagination, not social thesis — and he'll defend that view with considerable elegance.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has re-read Our Mutual Friend many times and still finds new things to stop her cold on every pass.
Today's segment is called The Comedy of Dust: Greed and Transformation — and we begin at the very opening of the novel, on the river at night.
What I love about the opening passages of this novel is that Dickens earns his comedy at the darkest possible cost.
Gaffer Hexam is pulling a body from the Thames — and yet what Dickens chooses to linger on, with almost theatrical relish, is what Gaffer does with the money he finds on the corpse.
The prose is so precise and so ritualised that it becomes almost ceremonial — which is, of course, the point.
Listen to this:
'He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon it once,—"for luck," he hoarsely said—before he put it in his pocket.'
Three identical actions, three times repeated — chink, blow, spit — and each one more transgressive than the last.
This is coin taken off a drowned man, and Gaffer is performing a luck ritual over it as though it were a harvest.
That triple repetition is doing so much structural work in such a tiny space — it's almost incantatory.
Dickens isn't describing a man washing his hands; he's describing a rite.
And notice the sequencing — 'his arms were wet and dirty, and he washed them over the side' — he washes himself in the river first, and then he washes the money.
The money and the man are morally equivalent in this world: both come out of the same filthy water, both need the same ritual cleansing.
And yet — and this is what makes Dickens Dickens — the comedy doesn't diminish the horror; it intensifies it.
'For luck, he hoarsely said' — that hoarse voice is doing tremendous work.
I think one must be careful not to flatten Gaffer into mere satire, however.
What Dickens shows us here is a man who has constructed a moral framework — however twisted — that makes his occupation bearable to himself.
The luck ritual is not cynicism; it is, if anything, a vestige of conscience — a whisper that what he does requires some form of propitiation.
Dr Johnson observed that the most obstinate sinners are those who have found private terms of accommodation with their sins.
Gaffer has done precisely that — and Dickens renders it with a compassion that the purely satirical reading would miss.
Edmund, I take that point — and it makes what comes later all the more affecting.
Because the novel ultimately argues that the only escape from the corruption of money is a kind of joyful refusal — and we see that most beautifully with Bella Wilfer.
There's a scene late in the novel where Bella kneels beside Mr Boffin and simply — I find this extraordinarily moving — she takes back everything she believed about him.
The language is deliberately childlike — Bella uses the word 'please' over and over like a child asking forgiveness — and it becomes a kind of incantation in reverse.
Here is what she cries out:
'Please I have found out something not yet mentioned. Please I don't believe you are a hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don't believe you ever for one single minute were!'
That exultant ringing laugh Dickens describes — you can hear it in the prose itself.

What strikes me structurally about that scene is that Bella's revelation rhymes with Gaffer's ritual — both are moments where a character performs a verbal act to change the moral weight of something.
Gaffer spits on the coin for luck; Bella speaks her 'please' to restore goodness.
One is comic-gothic; the other is comic-tender — and the novel holds both without apology.
And then there's the Sloppy reveal — which is pure theatrical farce — but even there the comedy carries genuine structural weight.
The novel has been about disguise and revelation from its first page — and here, at the end, an actual disguise is literally untied.
The Sloppy moment is one of the great comic coups of the novel, and it works because Dickens writes it with such precise physical detail.
Poor Wegg — who has spent the whole novel scheming and preening — turns his head and sees him.
Let me read it exactly as Dickens wrote it:
'Somebody else had come in quietly by the folding-doors. Turning his head, Wegg beheld his persecutor, the ever-wakeful dustman, accoutred with fantail hat and velveteen smalls complete.
Who, untying his tied-up broken head, revealed a head that was whole, and a face that was Sloppy's.'
'A face that was Sloppy's' — it lands like a punchline, and yet it's also a kind of justice.
I confess a particular fondness for the passage concerning Mr Boffin's correspondence — the taxonomy of beggars.
It is Dickens at his most Swiftian — the categories multiply with deadpan precision until the cumulative absurdity becomes overwhelming.
There is a line about the beggars' papers that I have never quite been able to forget.
'They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf.'
The simile is almost gratuitously precise — and quite devastating.
What I admire is that Dickens's satire here is not merely of the beggars — it is of the entire system that produces them and the sanctimony with which that system comforts itself.
And the passage is constructed as a catalogue — which is one of Dickens's most powerful rhetorical devices.
The 'inspired beggars,' the 'suggestively-befriended beggars,' the 'nobly independent beggars' — each category gets its own micro-narrative, its own absurd particular detail.
By the time you reach the man who requires an astronomical telescope to avoid permanent ruin, the comedy has become almost surreal.
And yet underneath it — as Edmund suggests — there is something genuinely bleak about the desperation being catalogued.
What brings all of this together for me — the greed, the comedy, the transformation — is that little meal scene with Bella, John, and her father.
It's the most tender passage in a novel full of tenderness, and it earns every drop of that feeling because we have sat through so much dust and corruption to get there.
Dickens describes it like this:

'It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, "Somebody's been drinking my milk!"'
'It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made.'
That fairy-tale frame — the hobgoblins, the forest — strips away all the novel's social machinery and leaves just the pleasure of being alive and fed and loved.
That is, I think, the essential movement of the whole novel — from the polluted river to the domestic hearth.
From Gaffer's coin spat upon for luck, to Bella's delicious repast made in poverty but in love.
The novel argues — and I think it argues convincingly — that character is the only currency that does not corrode.
Character as currency — and a currency that actually holds its value, which is more than can be said for anything else in this novel.

From Gaffer's ritual on the river to Sloppy's untied disguise, from the beggars' taxonomy to Bella's kneeling absolution — Dickens keeps asking what we are willing to do for money, and what we might become if we refuse it.
Thank you to Eleanor, Edmund, and Caroline — and we'll be back shortly with our next segment.

segments.title: Narratives Concealed: The Art of Harmon's Deception

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart — slowly, lovingly, and with full attention to every sentence.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside one of the novel's great structural gambits: the concealment at the heart of John Harmon's story.
Harmon is believed dead — and Dickens is in no hurry to correct that impression.
But before we follow the disguise itself, we have to understand what Harmon meant to the Boffins — and what the Boffins mean to the novel's moral architecture.
With me today: Dr Eleanor Hartley, who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — always looking for the hidden spring.
Sir Edmund Leigh, whose conviction that great fiction is fundamentally about individual character — not social critique — keeps the rest of us honest.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt, who has lived inside this novel since she was a teenager and still finds sentences in it that stop her cold.
Let's begin with the Boffins — and with what Dickens reveals about young John Harmon through their testimony.
What strikes me every time I return to these chapters is how brilliantly Dickens uses Boffin as a witness.
He is not an eloquent man — his grammar is unsteady, his metaphors are homespun — and yet the portrait he paints of the Harmon household is devastating.
There is this moment when he describes the old man's cruelty to Mrs Boffin.

"I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet — she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head — and send it spinning across the yard."
And then — almost as an afterthought — "Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her."
That repetition — "Dropped her" — is Dickens at his most controlled.
The second utterance says everything the first one couldn't quite land.
Yes — and notice that the comedy of the bonnet and the tragedy of Mrs Boffin going down are held in exact suspension.
The bonnet detail — black straw, perched on top as a matter of convenience — is absurd, deliberately so.
It disarms you before the violence lands.
This is Dickens managing emotional register with extraordinary precision — and doing it through a narrator who would never use the word 'precision.'
Boffin's artlessness is the instrument of Dickens's art.
And this matters structurally, because what Boffin is establishing here — without knowing it — is the moral context into which John Harmon will eventually return.
I think Eleanor is exactly right about the artlessness, and I should like to add: it is also a question of testimony under moral duress.
Boffin is speaking to a lawyer — Lightwood — and yet there is no calculation in him whatsoever.
He simply tells what he saw, because that is the kind of man he is.
Dickens understood — as Burke understood — that the moral weight of a testimony depends entirely on the character of the witness who bears it.
Boffin is not performing virtue.
He is simply being it — which is a much rarer and more affecting thing to put on a page.
And then Dickens gives us the memory of the child.
The scene where seven-year-old John Harmon comes to warm himself at the Boffins' fire before being sent abroad — I find it almost unbearable to read.
Dickens prepares it so carefully — the scanty clothes, the shivering wind, the sixpence the old man wouldn't allow for coach-money.
And then this — here is what Boffin says about Mrs Boffin's response:
"Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks."

"But seeing the tears come into the child's eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, 'I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!'"
The wide wide world — repeated like that.
It's a woman reaching for the largest thing she can imagine, and still feeling it isn't large enough.
And look at what that scene does to the novel's hidden structure.
We are reading this as backstory — as pathos — but we are also, if we are awake to it, reading the emotional warrant for John Harmon's later disguise.
He doesn't know the Boffins held him like this.
He is moving through the novel in the dark, and Dickens is lighting the rooms behind him one by one.
The reader is always slightly ahead of Harmon — and that dramatic irony is the engine of the whole deception plot.
I want to resist, slightly, the purely structural reading.
What moves me about this passage is not the machinery it drives, but the look on the child's face — "as if it was in pain, in agony."
And then the fact that Mrs Boffin could never revise it.
Whatever Boffin told her of how peacefully the boy had fallen asleep — according to her thoughts, he never changed that look.
That is not a narrative device.
That is the precise and terrible truth about how grief lodges in a devoted heart.
Which brings us naturally to Mrs Boffin's proposal — the plan to adopt an orphan and name him John Harmon — and what that tells us about how goodness actually operates in this novel.
The proposal is such a pure Mrs Boffin moment.
She wants to find an orphan child, give him John's name, provide for him.
And she frames it so disarmingly — "Say it's only a whim."
She almost pre-empts anyone who might dismiss her, and in doing so makes the impulse feel absolutely unassailable.

The full line is: "Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
There is such an exquisite irony locked inside this plan — which the reader cannot yet fully see.
The irony being that John Harmon is not, in fact, past all benefit — he is very much present, moving through the novel under an assumed name.
So Mrs Boffin's act of memorial is simultaneously, unknowingly, an act of prophecy.
And this connects to what Dickens says explicitly in Chapter Nine — one of those moments where the narrator steps forward and speaks in his own voice.
He describes the Boffins as people guided by "a religious sense of duty and desire to do right" — despite, as he puts it, ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities.
And then he states it as a law — not a sentiment, a law.
"For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never."
That is one of the most unambiguous moral declarations in the entire novel.
And I would simply say: thank goodness Dickens said it plainly.
We live in an age that is embarrassed by direct moral statement in fiction — that wants everything ironic, everything hedged.
Dickens had no such embarrassment.
He believed in good people — actually believed in them, not ironically.
And the Boffins — unpolished, grammatically wayward — are his proof.
The declaration that Good never stops — that it outlasts its doer — is not sentiment.
It is the theological spine of the whole plot.
And the plot doubles back on itself to prove it — because the other end of this strand of concealment is Gaffer Hexam's death.
Riderhood's discovery of the body is rendered in five words — perhaps five of the most economical words in the novel.
Riderhood has pursued Gaffer with accusations, has done everything to ruin him.
And then the recovered body turns out to be his quarry — already dead.
"Gaffer's done me. It's Gaffer!"
That is gothic comedy and moral consequence arriving in the same breath.
Evil — in the person of Gaffer — has stopped short at itself, exactly as Dickens said it would.
"Gaffer's done me" — that phrase is doing something extraordinary.
Riderhood means he's been cheated of his revenge — but the phrase also catches a kind of rueful admiration.
Gaffer has eluded him by dying — which is, when you think about it, the most complete evasion imaginable.
The river has been taking people from the very first page of this novel, and here it does so again.
Not as symbol — as event.
So we have concealment working at every level — Harmon concealing his identity, the river concealing its dead, Dickens concealing the moral pattern until the right moment to reveal it.
The art of deception in this novel is, paradoxically, an art of revelation.
Next, we'll follow Harmon further into the dark — into the interior monologue where he tries to reconstruct what happened on the night he was supposed to die.
Stay with us.

segments.title: London's Moral Landscape: Social Decay and Redemption

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Charles Dickens's last completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly — to see how it works.
Our Mutual Friend is a book about money, about rivers, about the very soil of London — and about what happens to human character when wealth arrives without warning.
Today we're exploring London's moral landscape — the social decay threaded through this novel, and the flickering possibilities of redemption within it.
With me are three exceptional readers of this novel, and I want to introduce them properly.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who has spent years studying how great fiction is architecturally built — sentence by sentence, image by image.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong devotion to the novel as a moral form gives him a perspective that is, to put it plainly, irreplaceable.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt has been reading and re-reading Our Mutual Friend since her teens, and brings to it the kind of intimacy that only repeated encounters with a great book can produce.
Let's begin where the novel's darkest currents run — on the river, and around the crime at the book's heart.
The scene in which Riderhood formally accuses Gaffer Hexam is one of those moments where Dickens seems to hold his breath.
Riderhood is not a trustworthy figure — we know that, and Dickens knows we know it.
And yet the accusation itself is framed with a terrible, almost biblical formality.
Listen to the rhythm of it — Riderhood insists on being taken down, as if he is dictating to posterity.
"I give information that the man that done the Harmon Murder is Gaffer Hexam, the man that found the body.
The hand of Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the hand that done that deed. His hand and no other."
That repetition — "the hand," "his hand," "no other" — has the cadence of an Old Testament condemnation.
Dickens is doing something morally precise here: he gives the most damning words to the least reliable mouth.
That is how guilt and innocence become entangled in this novel — and it is a thoroughly human entanglement.
Edmund, you've put your finger on something structural that I find absolutely thrilling about those scenes.
Dickens builds the accusation in layers — and then, in the very next passage, he gives us Riderhood's reported speech of Gaffer's supposed confession.
It's a double frame: we have Riderhood reporting what Gaffer said, inside a legal interrogation, inside the novel's narration.
Each frame is another layer of unreliability — and yet the words, when they come, hit with tremendous force.
The supposed confession Riderhood quotes is only six words long, but Dickens makes them ring like a tolling bell.
"There was foul play then. I done it for his money. Don't betray me!"
And then Riderhood adds — with that grotesque pedantry that is so perfectly his — "Those were the words as ever he used."
The grammar is broken, but the moral weight is absolute.
That's the kind of craft that makes me want to teach this novel forever.
What strikes me — and it strikes me every time I read it — is that the confession is reported inside a lie.
We never learn definitively whether Gaffer said those words at all.
But Dickens makes you feel the weight of the accusation so completely that the uncertainty becomes almost unbearable.
And I find Riderhood's scrupulousness — "I think he said in a score, but of that I am not positive, so take the lowest figure" — darkly funny.
He is meticulous about the small thing — the exact number of fine words Gaffer used — while lying about everything that matters.
That is a very precise portrait of a certain kind of moral corruption.
Quite so, and that precision is, I think, what separates Dickens from the purely polemical satirists of his age.
The corruption in this novel is never merely institutional — it is always personal, always rooted in individual weakness and vanity.
Which brings us, I think, to the Boffin material — which is a different kind of moral study altogether.
The flood of charitable solicitations that descends upon the newly wealthy Boffin is one of Dickens's great satirical set-pieces.
It is comedy, yes — but comedy that indicts an entire class of people who have confused the appearance of virtue with its substance.
Consider the Duke of Linseed's letter — lithographed by the hundred, Dickens tells us, yet presenting what he calls, with exquisite irony, a pale individuality of address.
The Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas.
Limited — that is the word that gives the game away.
As if the Duke has performed an act of generosity by confining his demand to a mere three guineas.
What I love technically about that passage is the sheer accumulation — the list of churches, parsonages, organs, children.
Dickens uses the enumerative sentence as a satirical weapon — more items, more absurdity, more indictment.
And then he pivots — beautifully — to that single fat private double letter with its ducal coronet.
The narrator calls it — and I think this is a perfect phrase — "Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
No verb. No apology. It lands like a thud — the physical weight of aristocratic presumption made almost comic.
Dickens is showing us that charity, in this world, is simply another currency — another form of the dust heap's transactions.
That phrase — "the gold dust of the Golden Dustman" — is one I keep coming back to.
It captures the whole paradox of Boffin's situation: he is both the joke and the target.
Everyone around him wants a piece of this man who made his fortune from other people's rubbish.
And there is something almost touching about Boffin's bewilderment — he genuinely does not understand why the world has suddenly become so very interested in him.
The novel is very clear that wealth, in this world, does not redeem anyone — it simply reveals them.
And what it reveals, in the case of those charitable noblemen, is not pretty.
Which is where the Wegg subplot becomes so wickedly relevant.
Wegg, of course, believes he has found a will that supersedes Boffin's inheritance — and he reads it to Venus with a kind of gleeful self-satisfaction.
The will itself is a masterpiece of misanthropic economy.
Let me read it — the logic of old Harmon's bequest is breathtaking in its contempt.

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
"Quite enough for him" — four words that contain an entire philosophy of punishment.
The old man is still controlling people from beyond the grave — and the novel's whole machinery turns on that fact.
One ought to note, though, that Wegg's triumphant reading of this document is itself a form of moral corruption.
He is not a man pursuing justice — he is a man pursuing advantage, and dressing it up in the language of legal rectitude.
Dickens understood — as Burke understood — that the forms of legitimacy can be captured by those who have no legitimate claim to them.
Wegg's relish in pronouncing "the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown" is comic, but the comedy has a cold edge.
It is the delight of a man who mistakes his scheming for cleverness and his greed for principle.
And what I find most devastating is that the will — even if it were genuine — reflects a world in which human connection has completely broken down.
"He has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family."
Those two facts, stated so flatly, are actually rather heartbreaking.
The whole novel is, in a sense, an attempt to repair that kind of damage — to find friendship, to find family, against the tide of a world that prices everything and values almost nothing.
The social decay is real and Dickens doesn't flinch from it. But the desire for something better is equally real.
That feels like exactly the right place to pause — on the tension between a world of calculation and the human impulse to transcend it.
We've heard how Dickens roots moral corruption in individual character — in Riderhood's slippery testimony, in the Duke's lithographed condescension, in Wegg's smug legalism.
Coming up, we'll turn to the question of what — if anything — Dickens offers by way of hope.
Stay with us.

segments.title: The Fog Lifts: Dickens's Final Synthesis

utterances.text: We've arrived at our final segment, and it feels right to take stock of what Dickens has built across this extraordinary novel.
We've moved through rivers of dust and money, through characters tested and transformed — and through a society Dickens dissects with surgical precision.
Three threads feel especially alive to me as we close: the pitiless machinery of poverty, the comedy of greed, and the moral imagination that holds it all together.
Caroline, you've been quietly waiting to talk about a passage involving a child — and I think it strikes at something central.
Yes — and it's a passage that stops you cold, if you're reading at any speed at all.
Lizzie Hexam is explaining to her brother Charley the circumstances of a sick little girl.
The father is a drunkard — 'a weak wretched trembling creature, falling to pieces, never sober' — the mother is dead.
And then Lizzie says something that absolutely pierces you.
'This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley.'
That parenthesis — 'if she ever had one' — is doing devastating work in a single breath.
Dickens embeds an entire unwritten history of deprivation in those five words.
That's such a precise observation, Caroline — and it speaks to a technique Dickens uses throughout the novel.
He'll make an enormous social statement, and then immediately undercut it with a tiny, almost throwaway qualification.
'If she ever had one' — structurally, that's the novel's whole argument in miniature.
The cradle is the symbol of a normal childhood, a normal beginning — and Dickens won't even grant her that certainty.
What's also worth noting is that this comes from Lizzie's mouth — not the narrator's.
Dickens routes the indictment through a character who is herself barely above the poverty line.
Which makes the compassion more earned, more true — and the accusation against society far harder to deflect.
I would not for a moment dispute the power of that passage.
But I think we should be careful not to read it purely as social polemic.
Lizzie's tenderness toward this child is a moral act — an act of goodness in a degraded world.
Dickens is always, at bottom, interested in what an individual chooses to do when surrounded by the worst that the world can offer.
Lizzie has come from the same river as her brother — yet she sees the child, she names the suffering, she cares.
The father is described as 'a good workman too, at the work he does' — and Dickens never quite removes that detail.
'A good workman too, at the work he does.'
Even in ruin, there is residual dignity — and Dickens, the moralist, insists we see it.
That's beautifully put, Edmund — and it makes me think about how the novel handles goodness without sentimentality.
Lizzie never asks to be admired for her compassion — she simply exercises it.
And I think that's what makes the contrast with the charity world so sharp — which brings me to Mr Boffin.
And Mr Boffin, in one of the novel's great comic set-pieces, has his own view of charity — or rather, of those who profit from its appearance.
Eleanor, this passage is yours — and I suspect you've been relishing it.
Relishing is exactly the right word — because this passage is pure Dickensian comic architecture.
Boffin is railing against the preposterous hierarchy of charitable titles, and the sentence just accumulates and accumulates.
Listen to how it builds.

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
It's a list that becomes its own satirical argument — the sheer proliferation of titles reveals the vanity of the whole enterprise.
'Deceased Patrons' is the killing stroke — they want credit even from beyond the grave.
And the image of Rokesmith sitting 'pretty well up to his neck' in these charity books is wonderfully absurd.
The comedy is unanswerable, I grant you.
But what strikes me is Boffin's genuine bewilderment — 'What the deuce is it all about?'
Boffin is a man of simple, direct moral instincts — he cannot comprehend why five shillings requires a title.
Dickens deploys him as a kind of moral barometer — uneducated, untitled, but sound.
He says — and I think this lands perfectly — 'If it ain't stark staring impudence, what do you call it?'
'If it ain't stark staring impudence, what do you call it?'
That is not social theory — that is moral clarity in the voice of plain English common sense.
I think Edmund's right that Boffin is a moral touchstone — but the craft is in how Dickens makes the comedy do the moral work.
We laugh at the list — but the laughter is indistinguishable from indignation.
That fusion of comedy and moral charge is one of the things Our Mutual Friend does better than almost any Victorian novel.
And where comedy tips into something darker — we have Silas Wegg.
Edmund, you've been sitting with Wegg's extraordinary scheme to blackmail Boffin — and I sense you have strong feelings.
Strong feelings, yes — though perhaps not the ones one might expect.
Wegg is, of course, a magnificent study in the corruption that self-interest produces when entirely unchecked by conscience.
The plan he lays out for Mr Venus is breathtaking in its elaborateness — and its moral squalor.
He proposes to keep Boffin in what the text calls — and the phrase is unforgettable —
'a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions.'
'Abject moral bondage' — Dickens has given us the vocabulary of slavery, applied to financial extortion.
It is a deeply serious moment, dressed in the finery of grotesque comedy.
What I find almost vertiginous about Wegg is the self-righteousness — the absolute conviction that he is owed all of this.
He addresses Venus throughout as 'comrade, brother, and partner' — the language of fellowship in service of pure predation.
And then there's the extraordinary moment at the end, where he offers to be corrected — 'it might be more according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds.'
'It might be more according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths.'
He's performing modesty while escalating his demands — and he appears entirely unaware of the comedy.
That kind of moral obliviousness is something Dickens reserves for his very finest villains.
The key word in that speech — and it appears repeatedly — is 'rights.'
'The rights of things' — Wegg has constructed an entire delusional legal and moral framework to justify extortion.
And Dickens lets the rhetoric inflate until it collapses under its own absurdity.
It's the same move he makes with the charity titles — satirical accumulation as a form of exposure.
The word 'Halves!' — delivered as if it were a legal verdict — is one of the funniest and most damning moments in the book.
Eleanor is right about accumulation — but I want to note something that is easily missed.
Wegg is, in his way, a perfectly consistent character.
His greed has a logic, a rhetoric, even a kind of dignity in its own dreadful terms.
Dickens doesn't make villains cartoonish — he makes them coherent.
And that is, if you will forgive a Johnsonian observation, what separates great moral fiction from mere moralising.
And on that distinction — between moral fiction and moralising — I think we've arrived at the heart of what makes Our Mutual Friend endure.
It holds together the darkest social realities and the most buoyant comedy — the child without a cradle and the patron beyond the grave — in a single, extraordinary vision.
Eleanor Hartley, Edmund Leigh, Caroline Woodcourt — thank you.
This has been Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

c30:p7.text:
‘When I came to England, attracted to the country with which I had none
      but most miserable associations, by the accounts of my fine inheritance
      that found me abroad, I came back, shrinking from my father’s money,
      shrinking from my father’s memory, mistrustful of being forced on a
      mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father’s intention in thrusting that
      marriage on me, mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious,
      mistrustful that I was slackening in gratitude to the two dear noble
      honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life or that
      of my heartbroken sister. I came back, timid, divided in my mind, afraid
      of myself and everybody here, knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my
      father’s wealth had ever brought about. Now, stop, and so far think it
      out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.
c30:p7.summary: John Harmon explains that he returned to England reluctantly, conflicted about his inherited wealth, fearful of a mercenary marriage, and anxious about his own character.
c30:p7.best_quote: I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife

c30:p9.text:
‘However, a sociable word or two on these mistakes became an easy
      introduction between us, and the weather was hot, and he helped me to a
      cool cabin on deck alongside his own, and his first school had been at
      Brussels as mine had been, and he had learnt French as I had learnt it,
      and he had a little history of himself to relate—God only knows how
      much of it true, and how much of it false—that had its likeness to
      mine. I had been a seaman too. So we got to be confidential together, and
      the more easily yet, because he and every one on board had known by
      general rumour what I was making the voyage to England for. By such
      degrees and means, he came to the knowledge of my uneasiness of mind, and
      of its setting at that time in the direction of desiring to see and form
      some judgment of my allotted wife, before she could possibly know me for
      myself; also to try Mrs Boffin and give her a glad surprise. So the plot
      was made out of our getting common sailors’ dresses (as he was able to
      guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer’s
      neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way, and doing whatever
      chance might favour on the spot, and seeing what came of it. If nothing
      came of it, I should be no worse off, and there would merely be a short
      delay in my presenting myself to Lightwood. I have all these facts right?
      Yes. They are all accurately right.
c30:p9.summary: John Harmon describes the scheme he and Radfoot devised to dress as common sailors, observe Bella Wilfer, surprise Mrs Boffin, and determine the authenticity of Bella's character before revealing himself to Lightwood.
c30:p9.best_quote: the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses (as he was able to guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way

c57:p80.text:
‘If you had any part—I don’t say what—in this attack,’ pursued
      the boy; ‘or if you know anything about it—I don’t say how much—or
      if you know who did it—I go no closer—you did an injury to me
      that’s never to be forgiven. You know that I took you with me to his
      chambers in the Temple when I told him my opinion of him, and made myself
      responsible for my opinion of you. You know that I took you with me when I
      was watching him with a view to recovering my sister and bringing her to
      her senses; you know that I have allowed myself to be mixed up with you,
      all through this business, in favouring your desire to marry my sister.
      And how do you know that, pursuing the ends of your own violent temper,
      you have not laid me open to suspicion? Is that your gratitude to me, Mr
      Headstone?’
c57:p80.summary: Charley systematically details how Bradley's suspected involvement in the attack on Eugene has compromised Charley's own reputation and trust.
c57:p80.best_quote: You know that I took you with me to his chambers in the Temple when I told him my opinion of you, and made myself responsible for my opinion of you.

c30:p22.text:
‘I have checked the calculation often, and it must have been two nights
      that I lay recovering in that public-house. Let me see. Yes. I am sure it
      was while I lay in that bed there, that the thought entered my head of
      turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some
      time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella. The
      dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that
      seemed to have fallen on my father’s riches—the fate that they
      should lead to nothing but evil—was strong upon the moral timidity
      that dates from my childhood with my poor sister.
c30:p22.summary: While recovering in the public-house, John Harmon decides to let himself remain dead for a time to prove Bella's character and avoid perpetuating his father's wealth's curse.
c30:p22.best_quote: the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.
c31:p1.best_quote: When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days.

c64:p101.text:
‘Now, scoundrel,’ he pursued, ‘I am going to finish. You supposed me just
      now, to be the possessor of my father’s property.—So I am. But
      through any act of my father’s, or by any right I have? No. Through the
      munificence of Mr Boffin. The conditions that he made with me, before
      parting with the secret of the Dutch bottle, were, that I should take the
      fortune, and that he should take his Mound and no more. I owe everything I
      possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness,
      goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin. And
      when, knowing what I knew, I saw such a mud-worm as you presume to rise in
      this house against this noble soul, the wonder is,’ added John Harmon
      through his clenched teeth, and with a very ugly turn indeed on Wegg’s
      cravat, ‘that I didn’t try to twist your head off, and fling  that  out of
      window! So. That’s the last short speech, do you understand?’
c64:p101.summary: Harmon explains that he owes his fortune entirely to Boffin's generosity, and his fury at Wegg's presumption against such a noble soul.
c64:p101.best_quote: I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin.

c28:p142.text:
‘Her heart—is given him, with all its love and truth. She would
      joyfully die with him, or, better than that, die for him. She knows he has
      failings, but she thinks they have grown up through his being like one
      cast away, for the want of something to trust in, and care for, and think
      well of. And she says, that lady rich and beautiful that I can never come
      near, “Only put me in that empty place, only try how little I mind myself,
      only prove what a world of things I will do and bear for you, and I hope
      that you might even come to be much better than you are, through me who am
      so much worse, and hardly worth the thinking of beside you.”’
c28:p142.summary: Lizzie pours out the lady's heart—her love and willingness to sacrifice herself for Eugene's redemption, expressing faith that her love might transform him into a better man.
c28:p142.best_quote: 'Only put me in that empty place, only try how little I mind myself, only prove what a world of things I will do and bear for you, and I hope that you might even come to be much better than you are, through me who am so much worse, and hardly worth the thinking of beside you.'

c19:p76.text:
‘I dare say my birds sing better than other birds, and my flowers smell
      better than other flowers. For when I was a little child,’ in a tone as
      though it were ages ago, ‘the children that I used to see early in the
      morning were very different from any others that I ever saw. They were not
      like me; they were not chilled, anxious, ragged, or beaten; they were
      never in pain. They were not like the children of the neighbours; they
      never made me tremble all over, by setting up shrill noises, and they
      never mocked me. Such numbers of them too! All in white dresses, and with
      something shining on the borders, and on their heads, that I have never
      been able to imitate with my work, though I know it so well. They used to
      come down in long bright slanting rows, and say all together, “Who is this
      in pain! Who is this in pain!” When I told them who it was, they answered,
      “Come and play with us!” When I said “I never play! I can’t play!” they
      swept about me and took me up, and made me light. Then it was all
      delicious ease and rest till they laid me down, and said, all together,
      “Have patience, and we will come again.” Whenever they came back, I used
      to know they were coming before I saw the long bright rows, by hearing
      them ask, all together a long way off, “Who is this in pain! Who is this
      in pain!” And I used to cry out, “O my blessed children, it’s poor me.
      Have pity on me. Take me up and make me light!”’
c19:p76.summary: Jenny recounts a memory or vision from her childhood of celestial children in white who appeared to her, asking 'Who is this in pain?' and offering her comfort and rest. They promised to return, and their refrain became her solace.
c19:p76.best_quote: 'Who is this in pain! Who is this in pain!' When I told them who it was, they answered, 'Come and play with us!'

c65:p104.text:
Not one other word did Bradley utter all that night. Not once did he
      change his attitude, or loosen his hold upon his wrist. Rigid before the
      fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with
      the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more
      haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being
      overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair
      degenerating.
c65:p104.summary: Bradley sits all night in rigid despair, his face aging, whitening, and degenerating as if being consumed by internal fire while Riderhood maintains his vigilance.
c65:p104.best_quote: Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating.

c1:p9.text:
It was not until now that the upper half of the man came back into the
      boat. His arms were wet and dirty, and he washed them over the side. In
      his right hand he held something, and he washed that in the river too. It
      was money. He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon
      it once,—‘for luck,’ he hoarsely said—before he put it in his
      pocket.
c1:p9.summary: Gaffer emerges from the water with money in his hand, which he washes, chinks, blows upon, and spits on 'for luck' before pocketing it.
c1:p9.best_quote: He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon it once,—'for luck,' he hoarsely said—before he put it in his pocket.

c63:p48.text:
‘John dear,’ said Bella, ‘you’re a good nurse; will you please hold baby?’
      Having deposited the Inexhaustible in his arms with those words, Bella
      looked hard at Mr Boffin, who had moved to a table where he was leaning
      his head upon his hand with his face turned away, and, quietly settling
      herself on her knees at his side, and drawing one arm over his shoulder,
      said: ‘Please I beg your pardon, and I made a small mistake of a word when
      I took leave of you last. Please I think you are better (not worse) than
      Hopkins, better (not worse) than Dancer, better (not worse) than
      Blackberry Jones, better (not worse) than any of them! Please something
      more!’ cried Bella, with an exultant ringing laugh as she struggled with
      him and forced him to turn his delighted face to hers. ‘Please I have
      found out something not yet mentioned. Please I don’t believe you are a
      hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don’t believe you ever for one
      single minute were!’
c63:p48.summary: Bella, having placed the baby in John's arms, kneels beside Mr Boffin and experiences a profound revelation: she retracts her earlier contemptuous words and declares her new understanding that he is essentially good, having designed his harsh performance to correct her character.
c63:p48.best_quote: Please something more! Please I have found out something not yet mentioned. Please I don't believe you are a hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don't believe you ever for one single minute were!

c64:p67.text:
Somebody else had come in quietly by the folding-doors. Turning his head,

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

      nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous
      low growlings of the alarming discovery, ‘Somebody’s been drinking  my

c8:p39.text:
‘And speaking of satisfactory,’ pursued Mr Boffin, ‘why, Lord save us!
      when we come to take it to pieces, bit by bit, where’s the
      satisfactoriness of the money as yet? When the old man does right the poor
      boy after all, the poor boy gets no good of it. He gets made away with, at
      the moment when he’s lifting (as one may say) the cup and sarser to his
      lips. Mr Lightwood, I will now name to you, that on behalf of the poor
      dear boy, me and Mrs Boffin have stood out against the old man times out
      of number, till he has called us every name he could lay his tongue to. I
      have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the
      claims of the nat’ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin’s bonnet (she wore,
      in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top
      of her head), and send it spinning across the yard. I have indeed. And
      once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should
      have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn’t thrown herself
      betwixt us, and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr
      Lightwood. Dropped her.’
c8:p39.summary: Boffin details how he and Mrs Boffin repeatedly defended young John Harmon against Old Harmon's cruelty, including an incident where Harmon struck Mrs Boffin and she collapsed, establishing their selfless advocacy for the boy.

Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.

c8:p43.text:
‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’
c8:p43.summary: Boffin recounts the last time he and Mrs Boffin saw young John Harmon, a seven-year-old being sent to a foreign school, including the poignant moment when Mrs Boffin wept while warming the boy by the fire and embraced him protectively, expressing a desire to save him—a memory that haunted her for years.

c9:p23.text:
Mrs Boffin pulled his nearest ear, in acknowledgment of this piece of
      philosophy, and then said, gradually toning down to a motherly strain:
      ‘Last, and not least, I have taken a fancy. You remember dear little John
      Harmon, before he went to school? Over yonder across the yard, at our
      fire? Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it’s come to us, I
      should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and
      give him John’s name, and provide for him. Somehow, it would make me
      easier, I fancy. Say it’s only a whim—’
c9:p23.summary: Mrs Boffin proposes adopting an orphan child, naming him John Harmon in memory of the young heir who drowned, thereby using their inherited fortune for redemptive good.
c9:p23.best_quote: Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him.

c9:p29.text:
These two ignorant and unpolished people had guided themselves so far on
      in their journey of life, by a religious sense of duty and desire to do
      right. Ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities might have been detected in
      the breasts of both; ten thousand vanities additional, possibly, in the
      breast of the woman. But the hard wrathful and sordid nature that had
      wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as
      little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst, had never been so
      warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it. In its
      own despite, in a constant conflict with itself and them, it had done so.
      And this is the eternal law. For, Evil often stops short at itself and
      dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.
c9:p29.summary: Dickens reflects that the Boffins, though ignorant and unpolished, have been guided by genuine religious duty and moral righteousness that even hardened souls cannot entirely resist.
c9:p29.best_quote: For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.

c14:p42.summary: Riderhood reveals that the recovered body is Gaffer Hexam, the missing man whom they had searched for all night.

c12:p93.text:
‘Now let me be took down again,’ said Riderhood, when he had turned the
      drowned cap over and under, and had brushed it the wrong way (if it had a
      right way) with his sleeve. ‘I give information that the man that done the
      Harmon Murder is Gaffer Hexam, the man that found the body. The hand of
      Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the
      hand that done that deed. His hand and no other.’
